screens.title: Image Descriptions (Alt Text)
screens.body:
Someone who is blind can't see an image - they rely on a screen reader speaking a text description in its place. Without one, the information the image was meant to convey is simply gone.

**Do:**

- Write a concise description of what the image shows and why it's there. Right-click the image and choose **View Alt Text**.
- Be meaningful, not repetitive - don't just repeat a caption or nearby text; describe what the image adds that isn't already said elsewhere.
- For a logo, use the format {{answer:word-q17}}"Logo: [Company Name]" - for example, "Logo: Benetech"{{/answer}}.
- For a complex image like a chart or graph, keep the alt text to a short summary and put the full description in the text right after the image.

**Don't:**

- {{answer:word-q1}}Start the description with "Image of..." or "Photo of..."{{/answer}} - a screen reader already announces that it's an image.
- Leave alt text blank on an image that conveys meaningful information - blank alt text should only ever be used for a genuinely decorative image (see the next screen).

**Keyboard shortcut:** Ctrl (PC) or Command (Mac) + Shift + F10 opens the right-click menu, then choose **View Alt Text**. On a PC you can also press Alt then Q to search, and type "Alt Text".

screens.title: Marking Decorative Images
screens.body:
Not every image carries meaning - a divider line, a border, or a purely visual flourish adds nothing a screen reader user needs to hear. Giving one of these a written description doesn't help; it just adds noise.

**Do:** Right-click the image, choose **View Alt Text**, and {{answer:word-q2}}check **Mark as decorative** instead of typing a description{{/answer}}. This tells screen readers to skip the image entirely, exactly as if it weren't there.

**Don't:** Write a description for an image that carries no real information, or leave its alt text blank without marking it decorative - a blank description still gets announced as "unlabeled image", which is more confusing than skipping it.

**Keyboard shortcut:** Ctrl (PC) or Command (Mac) + Shift + F10 opens the right-click menu, then choose **View Alt Text**.

screens.title: Use Real Headings, Not Bold Text
screens.body:
A common habit is to select some text, make it bold, and bump up the font size to make it look like a heading. To a sighted reader it looks like a heading - but it has no structural meaning at all to a screen reader. It's just larger, bolder text.

Screen reader users navigate long documents by heading - they can pull up a list of every heading and jump straight to the section they want, or jump to the next heading with a single key press. Text that only *looks* like a heading is invisible to that feature, turning the document into one long wall of text with no way to skim it.

**Do:** {{answer:word-q3}}Use Word's built-in Styles - Heading 1, Heading 2, and so on - from the **Home** tab's Styles gallery.{{/answer}}

**Don't:** Manually bold and enlarge text to fake a heading.

**Keyboard shortcuts (PC and Mac):** You don't need to select or highlight the text first - just click anywhere in the paragraph and press the shortcut; it applies to the whole paragraph.

- Ctrl/Command + Alt + 1, 2, or 3 for Heading 1, 2, or 3
- Ctrl/Command + Shift + N for Normal text

screens.title: Heading Hierarchy
screens.body:
Using real heading styles is the first step - using them in the right order matters just as much.

**Do:**

- Always start the document with a Heading 1 for the main title.
- {{answer:word-q4}}Follow a logical, sequential order: Heading 1, then Heading 2 for main sections, then Heading 3 for subsections of those.{{/answer}}
- Check your structure using the **Navigation Pane** (**View** tab): it shows a clickable, real-time outline of your document based on your heading styles, and is the fastest way to spot a heading applied to the wrong paragraph, or one you missed.

**Don't:**

- Use the **Title** style - it isn't announced by screen readers.
- Skip a level, such as jumping straight from a Heading 1 to a Heading 3. That creates a broken, confusing outline for anyone navigating by heading.

**Keyboard shortcut:** Ctrl/Command + F opens a sidebar with Find Results, Pages, and Headings tabs - the Headings tab is the Navigation Pane. (Mac users may need to assign this shortcut themselves.)

screens.title: Use Real Lists, Not Typed Bullets
screens.body:
Another common shortcut: typing an asterisk, a dash, or a number in front of each line to fake a list. {{answer:word-q5}}A screen reader just reads that character as text - it doesn't announce that the user has entered a list, or how many items are in it.{{/answer}} A properly formatted list, by contrast, announces something like "List, 5 items" before reading the entries, giving the listener real context.

**Do:** Use the **Bulleted List** or **Numbered List** buttons on the **Home** tab. (Word will sometimes auto-convert a manually typed list into a real one for you - if it does, that's fine, the goal is just a properly formatted list either way.)

**Don't:** Manually type *, -, or 1. in front of list items.

**Keyboard shortcuts:**

- PC: Alt + H (Home tab), then U for an unnumbered (bulleted) list or N for a numbered list
- Mac: Shift + Command + / to search, then type "Bulleted List" or "Numbered List"

screens.title: Accessible Tables
screens.body:
Tables come with a few specific accessibility traps: using them to lay out a page rather than to show data, merged or split cells breaking the predictable grid a screen reader expects, and missing headers leaving a listener with no idea what a given cell's data actually represents.

**Do:**

- {{answer:word-q6}}Use tables for data only - never to visually position content on the page.{{/answer}}
- Keep the structure simple: no merged or split cells. If your data seems to need them, it's better to split it into two or more simple tables.
- {{answer:word-q7}}Define your headers: click into the table, open **Table Design**, and check **Header Row** if the table has column headings, and **First Column** if it also has row headings.{{/answer}}
- For a long table, also turn on "repeat header row on each page" if that option is available.

**Keyboard shortcuts:**

- PC: Long-press Alt, then J then T (Table Design), then A for Header Row or M for First Column
- Mac: Shift + Command + / and search for "Repeat Header Rows"

screens.title: Meaningful Hyperlinks
screens.body:
Screen reader users often pull up a list of every link on a page, or jump from link to link with a single key press, hearing only the link text itself - not the surrounding sentence. {{answer:word-q12}}A list full of entries that just say "Click Here" gives them no way to tell which link goes where.{{/answer}}

**Do:**

- Make the link text itself describe the destination - for example, the entire phrase "Read the 2025 Annual Report" should be the link, not just the words "click here" tacked onto the end.
- Keep links in the standard, recognizable style: {{answer:word-q20}}blue text, underlined{{/answer}} - the underline matters just as much as the color, since color alone isn't a reliable way to convey meaning for every reader.

**Don't:** Use generic link text like "Click Here" or "Read More" on its own.

**Keyboard shortcut:** Ctrl/Command + K opens the hyperlink dialog on both PC and Mac.

screens.title: Use the Built-In Accessibility Checker
screens.body:
Word has a built-in **Accessibility Checker** under the **Review** tab (or via the status bar at the bottom of the window) on every platform. It's your first line of defense, and will catch a lot of what's covered in this module automatically - things like missing alt text, low contrast, and tables without defined headers.

It's a powerful assistant, but not a substitute for your own judgment: it can flag that alt text is *missing*, but {{answer:word-q15}}it can't tell you whether the alt text you wrote is actually *meaningful*{{/answer}}, or whether you used color as the only way to convey something. {{answer:word-q22}}Use it as a first pass, then read back through your own document with the concepts from this module in mind.{{/answer}}

**Keyboard shortcuts:**

- PC: Long-press Alt + R (Review), then A1, then A (Accessibility Checker)
- Mac: **Tools** menu > **Check Accessibility**, or Shift + Command + / and search for "accessibility"
